11-100.r: Navya-Nyaya school → founded by the work of Mithila scholar Udayana (Udayanacharya), followed by Gangesh; both (b) and (d) accepted.

11-101.r: 'Live well even by borrowing, for once cremated there is no return' → Charvakas, the materialist school rejecting afterlife.

11-102.r: Charvaka → 'the conscious body is the soul'; soul and body are the same, consciousness arises from the body.

11-103.r: Charvaka (Lokayata) → accepts only direct perception as a source of knowledge; rejects Vedas, Vedic rituals and the supernatural.

11-104.r: Charvaka (Lokayata) → highest value is Kama (pleasure); forerunner Ajita Kesakambali.
11-104.t: Not Moksha: Charvakas deny afterlife and liberation.

11-106.r: Nyaya Darshan → propagated by Gautama (Akshapada); main text 'Nyayasutra'; recognises 16 categories. Kapila → Sankhya; Jaimini → Purva Mimamsa.

11-110.r: Path to salvation: Nyaya → logical thinking; Mimamsa → Vedic rituals; Sankhya → real knowledge; Vedanta → self-knowledge. Founders: Gautam, Jaimini, Kapil, Badarayana.

11-111.r: Nyaya philosophy → knowledge (Gyana) is synonymous with Buddhi (cognition) and Upalabdhi (apprehension); valid means of knowledge = Pramana.

11-112.r: Correct pairs: Nyaya → Gautama; Vaisheshika → Kanada; Purva Mimamsa → Jaimini; Uttara Mimamsa → Badarayana.
11-112.t: Patanjali is Yoga and Kapila is Sankhya; the options swap them in.

11-114.r: Theory of Karma → Mimamsa (Karma / Purva / Dharma Mimamsa); Kumaril Bhatta links Purva Mimamsa and Vedanta.

11-115.r: Mimamsa → holds that the Vedas contain eternal truth; Purva Mimamsa = Karmakanda, Uttar Mimamsa = Gyankand.

11-116.r: Doctrine of Apurva → Mimamsa: an unseen force created by deeds (Karma) that links them to their results.

11-117.r: Atom theory → Vaisheshika school, founded by Maharishi Kanada.

11-118.r: Founder of Indian Atomism → Maharshi Kanad (Vaisheshika); matter is made of atoms, the smallest, invisible, indivisible unit; beginning of physics in India.

11-119.r: Six systems (Saddarsana) → Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta; Lokayata and Kapalika are not among them.

11-120.r: Bauddha → Nastika school, as it does not accept the Vedas as a valid source of knowledge; Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya are not Nastika.

11-121.r: Lokayata Darshan → Charvaka, the Indian materialist philosophy of material things and pleasures.

11-122.r: Advaita philosophy → principal exponent Adi Shankaracharya, who systematised earlier philosophers' work.

11-123.r: Shankara's Advaita Vedanta → Non-dualism: Brahman is the only reality, all else illusion; knowing Atman-Brahman identity gives Mukti.

11-124.r: Shankara (Adi Shankaracharya) → called 'Crypto-Buddhist' because he took many Buddhist ideas into Advaita.

11-125.r: Advaita Vedanta → Mukti is gained through Gyana (knowledge of the identity of Atman and Brahman).

11-126.r: Vishishtadvaita ('non-dualism with differentiation') → founded by Vaishnava saint Ramanujacharya (c. 1017-1137).

11-127.r: Not a Vedanta thinker → Abhinav Gupta. Vedanta scholars: Shankaracharya (8th century), Ramanuja (11th), Madhava (13th).

11-128.r: Eras reckoned from: Vikrama → 58 BC; Saka → 78 AD; Gupta → 320 AD (strictly 319); Kali → 3102 BC.

11-129.r: Vikram Samvat 58 BC (or 57); Saka Samvat 78 AD; Gupta era 319 AD; Muslim rule from 1192 AD (Ghori's Tarain victory). All correct.

11-130.r: Gadhaiya (Gandhaiya) → a silver coin made on the lines of Sassanian coins.

11-131.r: Badami rock inscription of Pulakesin I, Saka 465 → Vikrama Samvat 601 (465 + 78 + 58).
11-131.h: Saka to Vikrama: add 78, then add 58.

11-132.r: Malav Samvat → same as Vikram Samvat, also called Krit Samvat; begins 57 or 58 BC.

11-134.r: Puranas: Chandravansha rulers' prime place → Pratishthanpur (now Jhunsi, Prayagraj); capital set there by King Samvaram after a calamity at Prayag.

11-135.r: Maukharis (Gupta feudatories, originally from Gaya) → capital Kannauj; rulers Hari Varma, Aditya Varma, Ishan Varma, Sarva Varma, Graha Varma.

11-136.r: Wrong pair: Maukhari Sarvavarman's copper seal was found at Asirgarh fort (near Burhanpur, MP), not a Gaya copper plate.

11-137.r: Between Gupta decline and Harsha, North India held by → Later Guptas (Magadha), Pushyabhutis (Thanesar), Maukharis (Kanauj), Maitrakas (Valabhi). Not Paramaras or Yadavas (later).

11-138.r: Vardhana dynasty → founded by Pushyabhuti at Thaneshwar (per Banabhatta's Harshacharita); greatest ruler Harshavardhana.

11-139.r: Information on Harsha → Banabhatta's Harshacharita (main) and Kalhana's Rajatarangini; nothing in Kalidasa's or Harisena's works.

11-140.r: 'Harshacharita' → written by Banabhatta, Harsha's court poet; major source on the Vardhana dynasty.

11-141.r: Harsha's capital → Kannauj, shifted from Thanesar to help his sister Rajyashri govern Kannauj.

11-143.r: Harsha's two great assemblies → Kannauj (to show Mahayana's excellence; rulers of 20 countries) and Prayag (every fifth year, 'Mahamoksha' council; Hiuen Tsang attended the 6th).

11-145.r: Ruler of Assam in Harsha's time → Bhaskar Varman, last ruler of the Varman dynasty.

11-146.r: Pulakesin II (Chalukya) → stopped and defeated Harsha on the Narmada river; recorded in Aihole inscription and by Hiuen Tsang.

11-148.r: Pulakesin II's victory over Harsha → book (JPSC key) says 618 AD, from a copper plate reported in 2016; older view 630-634 AD (Aihole inscription, 634 AD).
11-148.c: Explanation first argues 630-634 AD and calls option (d) 634 AD nearest, then marks (b) 618 AD following the JPSC key.

11-149.r: Kushanas → Devaputra; Pulakeshin II → Dakshinapatheshvara; Harshavardhana → Sakalottarapathanatha; Samudragupta → Kaviraja.
11-149.h: Lord of the South (Pulakeshin) beat the Lord of all the North (Harsha).

11-150.r: Poet Banabhatta → born at Prithikuta village on the Son river (Aurangabad, Bihar; some say Kannauj); parents Chitrabhanu and Rajdevi; so 'None of the above'.

11-151.r: Hiuen Tsang → visited India in Harsha's reign; left Changan in 629 AD; wrote 'Sei-Yu-Kei' (Si-Yu-Ki).

11-153.r: Hiuen Tsang: roads not free of robbery (he was robbed); ordeals by fire, water, poison decided guilt; traders paid duties at ferries and barriers. Statements 2, 3 correct.

11-154.r: Hiuen Tsang was not sent by anyone: he came (629 AD) despite Tang emperor Taizong's ban; later wrote 'A Record of the Western Regions'.

11-155.r: Hiuen Tsang → Mathura was famous for cotton cloth; Thanesar prospered by trade; Ujjayini and Kannauj were also prosperous.

11-156.r: 'Kausheya' → silk, in Gupta and later Gupta periods.

11-157.r: Hiuen Tsang → studied at Nalanda University (637 AD), learning Yogashastra under Acharya Sheelbhadra.

11-158.r: Hiuen Tsang is remembered most for his travel record 'Sei-Yu-Kei', full of information on ancient India.

11-159.r: Hiuen Tsang (Harsha's time) → also visited Bhinmal; his travel record is 'Si-Yu-Ki'.

11-161.r: I-tsing (Chinese traveller, 671-695 AD) → came by the western sea route from Canton and returned via Sumatra; none of the given dates fits.

11-162.r: Hundi (post-Harsha sources) → a bill of exchange used in trade and credit.

11-163.r: Chinese writers called India 'Yin-tu' or 'Thian-tu' (variants of Hindu / Sindhu).
11-163.t: Si-Yu-Ki is Hiuen Tsang's travel record, not a name for India.

11-164.r: Nalanda University → destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khalji's army (Muslims) at the end of the twelfth century; final blow to Buddhism's decline in India.

11-165.r: Nalanda (Bihar) → most ancient monastery among options; linked to Buddha-Mahavira days, but excavations show occupation only from the Gupta period.

11-167.r: Post-Gupta main business centre → Kannauj (shifted from Ujjain); Harsha's capital; later contested by Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas.

11-168.r: Post-Gupta agrarian structure → feudalism: land grants created landlord intermediaries and dependent peasants; A and R true, R explains A.

11-169.r: Both false: Fa-Hien came in Chandragupta II's reign (not to Kanishka's council); Harsha already leaned to Buddhism and patronised Mahayana after meeting Hiuen-Tsang.

11-171.r: Correct dates: Fa-Hien 399-414 AD (in India 402-412); Hiuen-Tsang 629-645 AD; I-tsing 671-695 AD (not 679); Al-Masudi 915-16 AD (not 957).
11-171.c: Answer not printed; by the explanation both (c) and (d) are wrongly matched.

11-172.r: Order of visitors → Fa-Hien (402-412 CE), Hiuen Tsang (629-645), I-tsing (671-695), Al-Biruni (1017-1030).

11-173.r: Multan Sun temple → mentioned by Hiuen Tsang, Al Masudi and Alberuni; pilgrimage to Sambapur linked to Sun worship. Both correct.

11-174.r: Indian feudal system → administration based on control and possession of land, and lord-vassal ties; not a strong centre with very weak local power. Statements 2, 3.

11-175.r: Sondani (Sondhni) inscription of Yashodharman → composed by Vasula Kavi; records his victories and rule.

11-176.r: Shankaracharya (8th century, born Kaladi, Kerala) → set up four religious centres, revived Hinduism against Buddhism-Jainism, propagated Advaita Vedanta; he did NOT name Prayag 'Teerthraj'.

11-178.r: Adi Shankaracharya's four maths → Joshimath, Dwarka, Puri, Sringeri; Mansarovar is not in the Char Dham.
